title: Natty or not (.com): Jeff Nippard
summary: Roasts the Natty or Not website's article claiming Jeff Nippard is enhanced. He attacks its body fat estimates (DEXA, scales), the FFMI 25 cutoff from a flawed 1995 study, straw-man arguments, misunderstanding of steroid gains, short-lifter aesthetics, 'world-class' strength claims and the '3D look', and the claim that training can't break a natural limit. He concludes Nippard is 100% natural and that the natural limit doesn't exist.

claims.claim: Natty-or-not analyses rely on impossible stats: 165 lbs at 8% body fat for someone 5'5" would imply implausible lean mass; Nippard in that video looked 13-14%, not 8%.
Electronic body fat scales are not accurate at all; they tell him 12-14% every time.
DEXA scans are not accurate either and can be skewed by manipulating water intake, especially across repeated scans; being used by elite labs doesn't make them accurate.

The FFMI natural cutoff of 25 comes from a 1995 study of ~150 athletes (half on steroids) that didn't control training regimen or years trained, and athletes don't train for maximal muscle, so the cutoff is worthless.
Joint size doesn't predict overall frame: his wrists are under 6.5 inches, yet his knees are average and ankles above average.
His main problem with FFMI is body fat: we can't measure it well, and every percent of underestimated fat gets counted as muscle, pushing naturals above 25.
You can't base an analysis on hypothetical steroid results: response, side effects and gains are unknown, and there is almost no data on PED effects in advanced athletes.
Most people who jump on PEDs are novices, not even late intermediates, pushed by people saying nothing is possible naturally; almost no one trains 10 years before using.
Mass-gaining steroids are 'wet' compounds: you gain muscle but also fat and water, not pure lean mass; the water and fat distribution just look better than natural weight gain.
Classic bodybuilders like Serge Nubret, Schwarzenegger and Franco Columbu were never near 5% body fat; people vastly underestimate the fat a muscular male carries.
Accurately understanding body fat percentage is the most pivotal theme for natural bodybuilding and natty debates.
The most muscular bodybuilder doesn't necessarily win: muscle attachments, flow and posing matter more than weight; otherwise Big Ramy would win every year.
Enhanced mass takes a long time on drugs because the muscle must stay in that hormonal profile to accumulate tonnage.
Taller men have higher potential for total mass, but it takes much longer to fill their frame and they face leverage issues; tall lanky lifters can become monsters with time.
He is 6 feet with medium-length limbs and a small frame.
Being short is an advantage in bodybuilding: smaller segments look more 3D and big with less muscle; the same arm size looks huge on a 5'5" man and flat on a 6'5" man.
Short competitors get dwarfed next to someone 40 lbs heavier and 6-7 inches taller, but since judging is about aesthetics and flow, giant killers like Lee Priest exist.
Nippard's lifts (~200 kg squat, 160 kg bench, 205 kg deadlift at ~150 lbs) are strong but nowhere near world class, and his slow progress since points to being natural.
Pound-for-pound strength favors smaller, lighter lifters; even Wilks-type scoring favors very light competitors.
The '3D Photoshop look' is achievable with good lighting, angles and dropping 4-5% body fat; naturals can have capped delts, just not the bulky popping delts of steroid users.
Drug tests mean nothing because they can be passed, which is why natty status can never be resolved and must be judged from objective facts, not FFMI or 3D delts.
Big YouTube fitness channels must collab with fake natties because they have audiences; they represent a male power fantasy that attracts young men who are easy to swindle.
Saying 'natural' in a title is not evidence of being enhanced; that reverse logic is used by people looking for excuses for being small.

A muscle's capacity for protein synthesis grows as it gets bigger (more fibers), so the cycle of training, growth and more synthesis means there is no natural limit; progressive training forces adaptation, slowly but surely.
In his opinion Jeff Nippard is 100% natural, simply someone who has trained a long time and understands how it works.
